unit.title: Use advanced features of computer applications

summary: This unit takes you beyond the basics of office software. You will learn to produce long, well-organised documents with styles, contents pages, headers, footers and section breaks; send personal letters with mail merge; review documents with Track Changes and comments; build spreadsheets with formulas, functions, charts and data tools; make clear presentations; use a simple database; and save, share, link and protect your files properly.

blocks.p: Every trade now runs on documents: quotations, job sheets, price lists, client letters, stock lists, training slides and customer records. This unit teaches the features that turn a few typed pages into professional work and save hours of retyping. It is shared by several programmes, so the examples come from electrical contracting, salons, hotels, workshops and small offices. Menu names differ a little between programs and versions: look for the same feature under a similar name, and ask your instructor.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like at work
rows: Use heading styles, an automatic table of contents, headers, footers, page numbers, section breaks, page orientation and templates.
Use Find and Replace, keyboard shortcuts and tables.
Make personal letters, labels or emails from one letter and a list of clients.
Use Track Changes and comments, and produce a clean final version.
Write formulas and functions, use relative and absolute references, and find and fix errors.
Sort, filter, apply conditional formatting, freeze headings, make charts and set up printing.
Use the slide master, layouts, transitions, animations and speaker notes, and keep slides clear.
Explain tables, fields, records and primary keys, and use forms, queries and reports.
Paste, link and embed between programs, and save work as PDF.
Name and store files clearly, save often, back up, and protect private information.

blocks.h: Finding your way round the screen

ul: The **ribbon** (or toolbar) is the strip of tabs and buttons across the top of the window. Each tab holds a group of related tools, such as Insert or Review.
The **status bar** at the bottom shows the page number, word count or, in a spreadsheet, the sum of the selected cells.

A **screenshot** is a picture of the screen saved as an image. Use the Print Screen key or the computer's snipping tool; on a phone, the button combination your phone uses. Screenshots are useful for showing a problem to IT support or recording your work.

head: Shortcut (Windows; Cmd on a Mac)
What it does
rows: Undo the last action / redo it
Find / Find and Replace (in many programs)
Insert a page break in a word processor
Start a slide show from the beginning in many presentation programs

blocks.note: Work on the Centre's or your employer's computers only as their rules allow, and use made-up names in practice work, never real clients' details.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **style** is a saved set of formatting (font, size, colour, spacing) with a name, such as Normal, Heading 1 or Heading 2. Apply **Heading 1** to chapter titles and **Heading 2** to the parts inside a chapter, and keep body text in Normal.

ul: Every heading of the same level looks the same, and if you change the style once, every heading of that kind changes.
The program knows which lines are headings, so it can build a **table of contents** and a navigation pane from them.
Making a title bold and large by hand does **not** make it a heading: the contents page will not find it.

blocks.p: Put the cursor where the contents should go and insert an **automatic table of contents**. The program builds it from the heading styles, with page numbers. When you add, move or rename headings, use **Update Table** (update the entire table) so that the titles and page numbers stay correct. Never type a contents page by hand in a long document.

ul: The **header** is the area at the top of every page; the **footer** is the area at the bottom. Text in them, such as the business name, repeats on every page.
Insert page numbers as a **field** in the header or footer, so that they update by themselves when pages are added or removed. Never type numbers by hand.
Use **Different First Page** to leave the header and number off a cover page.

blocks.p: A **section break** divides a document into parts that can each have their own layout: orientation, margins, columns, headers, footers and page numbering. A page break only starts a new page; a section break starts a new part with its own settings.

head: You want
Do this
rows: One wide table on a landscape page in a portrait booklet
Put a section break (next page) before and after the table, then set only that section to landscape.
No page number on the cover and contents, and page 1 on the first chapter
Put a section break after the contents; in the new section unlink the header and footer from the previous section ('Link to Previous' off) and set page numbering to start at 1.
Two columns for one part of a newsletter
Put a continuous section break before and after that part and set two columns there.

ul: **Portrait**: the page is taller than it is wide; normal for letters and reports. **Landscape**: wider than it is tall; good for wide tables, charts and price lists.
Set margins and paper size (Letter or A4, as the business uses) before you lay out the pages.
Use **Print Preview** to check the whole document before printing or saving as PDF.

blocks.p: A **template** is a ready-made layout for new documents, such as a letterhead, a quotation or a job sheet, with the logo, styles and fixed text already in place. Opening a template makes a new document, so the template itself is not changed by mistake. Templates make every document from the business look the same.
**Find and Replace** changes every copy of a word or phrase in one go. Use the options carefully:

ul: **Match case**: finds 'JPS' but not 'jps'.
**Find whole words only**: replacing 'amp' with 'ampere' will not also change 'lamp' or 'camp'.
Click **Replace** to check each one before changing it; use **Replace All** only when you are sure, then read the result. Ctrl+Z undoes a Replace All.
Use a table, not spaces or tabs, to line up a price list or schedule. Mark the top row as a header row that repeats on every page for long tables.
Insert pictures from the business's own photos, or ones you have permission to use. Set text wrapping so that the picture sits where you want it, and add a short caption.

sections.title: Word processing: mail merge and reviewing

blocks.p: **Mail merge** makes many personal letters, envelopes, labels or emails from **one main document** and **a list of people**. Each letter gets that person's own details, so 200 reminder letters take minutes, not days.

head: Part
What it is
rows: The letter (or label or email) with the text that is the same for everyone.
The list of names and details: a table, a spreadsheet or a database, with one row for each person and a heading on each column.
A placeholder in the main document, such as «FirstName», where each person's detail is put in.
The finished letters, printed, emailed or saved as a new document.

flow: Prepare the data source: one row per person, a clear heading on every column, no blank rows
Check the data: spelling, empty cells, the same date format throughout
Start the mail merge in the word processor and choose the type: letters, envelopes, labels or emails
Connect the main document to the data source
Type the text that is the same for everyone, and insert merge fields where the personal details go
Filter or sort the recipients if only some people should get the letter
Preview several letters, including the first and the last, and fix any problems
Finish the merge: print, email, or make a new document to check first
Save the main document and the data source so that they can be used again

blocks.note: A gap or a wrong detail in the preview almost always comes from the **data source**, such as an empty cell, a name typed in the wrong column or extra spaces. Fix it in the list, not in each letter, and preview again.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Track Changes** marks every edit so that the writer can see it and decide whether to keep it. Turn it on **before** the document is shared for review. Each reviewer's insertions and deletions show in colour with their name.

flow: The writer turns on Track Changes and shares the document
Reviewers edit the text and add comments
The writer goes through each change and clicks Accept or Reject
The writer answers each comment, then resolves or deletes it
When nothing is left, the writer turns Track Changes off
The final copy is checked with no markup showing and saved with a new version name

blocks.p: A **comment** is a note in the margin that asks a question or makes a suggestion **without changing the text**, for example 'Check this price with the supplier'. Comments can be answered, resolved and deleted. Delete them all before a document goes to a client.

blocks.note: Turning off the display of markup only hides the changes: they are still in the file and the client can see them. Accept or reject every change and delete every comment before you send a final copy.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The spreadsheet file, which holds one or more sheets (worksheets).
A line of cells running down the sheet, named A, B, C …
A line of cells running across the sheet, numbered 1, 2, 3 …
One box, named by its column and row, such as B4.
A group of cells, written with a colon: B2:B10 means B2 to B10.
Shows what is really in the selected cell: the formula, not just its answer.

blocks.p: A formula works something out. It **starts with an equals sign (=)**, and uses cell references so that the answer changes when the numbers change.

**Percentages.** A sale price after a discount is the price × (1 − the discount). For example, a J$4,800 item at 15% off: **=4800*(1-15%)** gives **J$4,080**. The discount itself is =4800*15%, which is J$720.

**Order of operations**: brackets first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. So **=4+6*3** gives 22 (6 × 3 = 18, then + 4), but **=(4+6)*3** gives 30. Use brackets whenever you mean something to be worked out first.

head: Function
What it does
Example
rows: Counts cells that are not empty, text included
Counts cells that meet a condition
Gives one of two results, depending on a test
Rounds to a number of decimal places

blocks.p: In the IF example, C2 is the number in stock and D2 the reorder level: if the stock is at or below the reorder level the cell shows Reorder, otherwise OK. Text in a formula goes in double quotation marks.

ul: A **relative** reference, such as B2, changes when the formula is copied. =B2*C2 in D2, copied down to D3, becomes =B3*C3. That is what you want for line totals.

An **absolute** reference has dollar signs, such as **$F$1**, and does not change when copied. Use it for one fixed value that every row uses, such as a discount rate or the GCT rate kept in one cell.
A **mixed** reference, such as $F1 or F$1, fixes only the column or only the row.
In many programs, pressing F4 while the cursor is in a reference cycles through these forms.

blocks.p: **Example.** A quotation has line totals in D2:D15 and a trade discount rate of 5% in F2. In E2 type **=D2*$F$2** and copy it down: D2 becomes D3, D4 … but $F$2 stays fixed. If you typed =D2*F2, the copy in E3 would become =D3*F3, which points to an empty cell and gives 0.

blocks.note: Keep rates such as discount and GCT in their own labelled cells and point to them with absolute references. When the rate changes, you change one cell, not every formula. For GCT, use the current rate your supervisor gives you.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The **fill handle** is the small square at the bottom-right corner of the selected cell. Drag it, or double-click it, to copy a formula down a column, or to continue a series such as 1, 2, 3 or Jan, Feb, Mar.

head: Error
Usual cause
Fix
rows: Dividing by zero or by an empty cell
Check the cell you divide by; fill it in, or use IF to skip empty rows.
Text where a number is needed, such as 'ten' or a number with a space
Type the number as a number.
A function name typed wrongly, such as =SUMM(
The formula points to a cell that was deleted
Rewrite the formula with the right cells.
The column is too narrow to show the number

blocks.note: Check a formula's answer once with a calculator or by estimating. A spreadsheet is only as right as the formula you typed.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Format money as **currency** or accounting with two decimal places (J$ for Jamaican dollars), so that totals line up and read clearly.
Format rates as **percentages**; dates in one clear format throughout.
Formatting changes only how a number looks, not its value: 12.346 formatted to two places still holds 12.346. Use ROUND when the stored value must be rounded.

head: Tool
What it does
Example
rows: Puts rows in order by one or more columns. Select the whole table, or one cell in it, so that each row stays together.
A stock list sorted by quantity, smallest first, puts the items running low at the top.
Shows only the rows that match your choice and hides the rest without deleting them.
Show only jobs in one parish, or only hair products, then clear the filter to see everything.
Changes a cell's colour or style when its value meets a rule.
Stock cells turn red when the quantity falls to the reorder level or below.
Allows only certain entries in a cell, often from a drop-down list.
The Unit column accepts only 'each', 'm' or 'box', so nobody types 'mtr' or 'metres'.
Keeps the heading row or first column in view while you scroll.
Column headings stay at the top of a 300-row client list.

blocks.note: Never sort only one column of a table: the other columns stay where they were, and each item ends up with the wrong price. Select the whole table, or a single cell inside it, before you sort.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Chart
Best for
Example
rows: Sales of each product, or the cost of each material
Monthly sales of cable over a year
Parts of one whole, with only a few slices
Each service's share of a salon's sales

flow: Set out the data in a table with headings
Select the headings and the data
Insert the chart type that suits the question
Add a clear title and axis titles with units, and a legend if there is more than one series
Check that the chart shows the data correctly, then move it so it does not cover the table

ul: Use **Print Preview** first: wide sheets often spill onto extra pages.
Set the **print area** to print only the part you need.
Choose **landscape** and **fit to one page wide** for wide sheets.
Set **print titles** so that the heading row repeats on every printed page.
Add a header or footer with the file name, date and page number.

blocks.p: You can lock cells and **protect the sheet** so that others can type in the input cells, such as quantities, but cannot change the formulas by mistake. A password can be added; keep it safe, because a forgotten password may lock you out too.

ul: Each page of a presentation is a **slide**. Plan the content first: one main idea to each slide, in a sensible order.

The **slide master** sets the look of every slide in one place: background, fonts, colours, logo and footer (such as the slide number). Change the master and every slide changes, including slides added later.
A **layout** arranges placeholders on a slide, such as Title and Content, Two Content or Title Only. Choose the layout that fits the content instead of drawing your own text boxes.
A **theme** is a set of matching colours, fonts and effects for the whole presentation.

head: Feature
What it does
Good practice
rows: The effect **between** slides, as one slide replaces the next
Use one simple transition for the whole show.
Makes an **item on a slide** appear, move or disappear
Use a few, only where they help, such as showing points one at a time. Many different effects distract the audience.

ul: **Speaker notes** hold the presenter's reminders under each slide; the audience does not see them on the screen.
**Presenter view** shows the presenter the current slide, the next slide, the notes and a timer on the laptop, while the projector shows only the slide.
**Handouts** print several slides to a page for the audience to take away.

head: Do
Avoid
rows: A few short points on each slide
Long paragraphs that the audience reads instead of listening
Large text: often at least about 24 pt for points and larger for titles
Small print that cannot be read from the back of the room
Strong contrast: dark text on a light background, or light on dark
Pale text on a busy picture
Many fonts and colours on each slide
Clear photos and diagrams you have permission to use
Blurred pictures, or pictures copied from the internet without permission
Alternative (alt) text on pictures, for people who use screen readers

ul: Run the show in **Slide Show view** from the beginning, to see it as the audience will: check the order, spelling, animations and timing.
Check that the laptop works with the projector or screen, and bring a copy on a flash drive or in cloud storage.
Rehearse with the speaker notes, and time yourself.

blocks.p: A **database** stores information so that it can be searched, sorted and reported. A client list of thousands of people, with their jobs or appointments, is far easier to manage in a database than in a stack of cards or one long spreadsheet.

head: Part
What it is
Example (an electrical contractor)
rows: Stores the data on one subject, in rows and columns
A Customers table; a Jobs table
One kind of detail, a column
All the details about one item, a row
A field whose value is different for every record
A screen for entering or viewing one record at a time
The New Customer form at the front desk
A search for the records that meet your conditions
All jobs in Portland since 1 June
Sets out data neatly for printing, with groups and totals
Jobs and charges for the month, totalled by parish

head: Data type
Use it for
rows: Names, addresses, and numbers that are not used in sums, such as phone numbers and IDs
Money, such as charges in J$
Dates of jobs and appointments, so that they sort and search correctly
Something that is either true or false, such as 'Paid'

blocks.note: Store phone numbers as **text**, not numbers: they are never added up, and a number field may drop a leading zero or reject a plus sign, brackets or dashes, as in (876) 555-0123.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A business usually keeps customers and jobs in separate tables, linked by the primary key. Each job record carries the CustomerID of the customer it belongs to. Two customers with the same name are kept apart by their different IDs, and each customer's details are typed only once, however many jobs they have.

A query picks out records using **criteria** on one or more fields. For example, Appliance = 'Refrigerator' and Date on or after 1 June finds every fridge job since June. The query can be saved and run again next month, and a report can be built on it for printing.

ul: Type data the same way every time ('St Ann', not sometimes 'St. Ann' and sometimes 'Saint Ann'), or a query will miss records. Drop-down lists on forms help.
Check new records for mistakes before saving, and never delete a record without checking that nothing else depends on it.

sections.title: Using applications together, and looking after files

head: Method
What happens
Use it when
rows: The item is copied with its formatting
Everyday copying within or between documents
Only the words come across, without the formatting
Copying from a web page or email into a styled document
An image of the item; it cannot be edited or updated
A chart that must never change
A copy of the data travels inside the document and can be edited there, but does not change when the original file changes
Sending a document to someone who does not have the source file
The document shows the data from the source file and can be updated when the source changes
A monthly report whose chart must follow the latest figures

blocks.note: A link depends on the source file staying where it was. If you move or rename the spreadsheet, the link breaks. Keep both files together, update the links before printing, and break the links (or save as PDF) before sending the document outside the business.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Applications also work together through **mail merge** (a spreadsheet or database as the data source), by **importing** a CSV file of figures into a spreadsheet or database, and by **saving as PDF**.

A **PDF** looks the same on any computer or phone, prints as you laid it out, and is hard to change by accident. Save quotations, price lists, booklets and reports as PDF before sending them to clients; keep the original file to edit later.

ul: Give every file a **clear name** that says what it is, for whom and when, such as Quote_HarrisResidence_2026-11-10. A date written year-month-day sorts in order.
Keep files in a sensible **folder structure**, such as one folder per year, then per client or job.
Save **early and often** (Ctrl+S). Use Save As, with a new version number (v1, v2), when you want to keep the earlier version.
Close files properly, and never work straight from an email attachment: save it to the right folder first.

blocks.p: A **backup** is a second copy of your files kept somewhere else, so that work is not lost if the computer fails, is stolen, catches a virus or is damaged by a power surge or flood. A common rule is **3-2-1**: three copies of important files, on two different kinds of storage, with one kept away from the office (for example in the business's cloud storage). Check now and then that you can open a file from the backup.

blocks.note: Power cuts and surges are common in Jamaica, especially in thunderstorm and hurricane seasons. Save often, use a UPS or surge protector for the office computer as the business decides, and keep backups away from the computer itself.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Client details such as names, addresses, phone numbers, health notes and payments are private. **Jamaica's data protection law** expects businesses to keep personal data secure and use it only for the purpose it was collected for.
Protect files that hold client details with a strong **password**, and share them only with staff who need them.
Lock the screen when you leave the computer (Windows key + L on Windows) and log off at the end of the day.
Do not send work files to your personal email or phone. Shred printed copies you no longer need.
Keep the security software up to date and do not open unexpected attachments.
Sit with your back supported, feet flat, the top of the screen at about eye level and your wrists straight.
Rest your eyes: every 20 minutes or so, look at something far away for about 20 seconds.
Keep drinks and food away from the keyboard, and cables off the floor where people walk.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can apply heading styles and insert and update an automatic table of contents.
I can add a header, a footer and automatic page numbers, and leave them off a cover page.
I can use section breaks to put one landscape page in a portrait document or restart page numbering.
I can use a template and use Find and Replace with its options.
I can carry out a mail merge from a data source and fix problems found in the preview.
I can use Track Changes and comments, and produce a clean final copy.
I can write formulas that follow the order of operations, and use SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, COUNTIF, IF and ROUND.
I can explain relative, absolute and mixed references and use the fill handle.
I can recognise #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #NAME?, #REF! and ##### and fix them.
I can sort, filter, apply conditional formatting and data validation, and freeze panes.
I can choose and make a suitable chart, and set up a sheet for printing.
I can use the slide master, layouts, transitions, animations, speaker notes and presenter view.
I can explain tables, fields, records, primary keys, forms, queries and reports, and choose data types.
I can paste, link and embed between applications and save work as PDF.
I can name, store, back up and protect files properly.

terms: Absolute reference
A cell reference with $ signs, such as $F$1, that stays fixed when a formula is copied.
Comment
A note in the margin that asks or suggests something without changing the text.
Conditional formatting
Changing a cell's look automatically when its value meets a rule.
Data source
The list of names and details used in a mail merge.
Embedded object
A copy of data from another program kept inside a document; it does not update.
Field
In a database, one kind of detail (a column); in a mail merge, a placeholder for a detail.
Filter
Showing only the rows that match a choice, without deleting the others.
Footer / header
The areas at the bottom and top of every page.
Linked object
Data shown from another file that updates when that file changes.
Mail merge
Making many personal documents from one main document and a list.
Primary key
A field whose value is different for every record, such as a customer number.
Query
A database search for records that meet certain conditions.
Range
A group of cells, such as B2:B10.
Record
In a database, all the details about one item (one row).
Section break
A divider that lets part of a document have its own layout and page numbering.
Slide master
The slide that sets the design for every slide in a presentation.
Style
A saved, named set of formatting, such as Heading 1.
Template
A ready-made layout from which new documents are made.
Track Changes
A feature that marks every edit so that it can be accepted or rejected.
Workbook
A spreadsheet file that holds one or more sheets.

c1.title: A rewiring quotation in Falmouth
c1.text: Trainee Odette is building a materials quotation in a spreadsheet for a house rewire in Falmouth, Trelawny, for her supervisor Mr Roy Dixon. Column A holds the item, B the quantity, C the unit price in J$ and D the line total, for 14 items in rows 2 to 15. The subtotal is in D17. The GCT rate (the current rate) is in F1, and a 5% trade discount for this client is in F2.

c2.title: A customer booklet in Black River
c2.text: Trainee Damion is producing a 12-page customer booklet, 'Caring for your solar water heater', for an installer in Black River, St Elizabeth. It has a cover page, a contents page and six chapters, and on page 9 a wide price table that will only fit across a landscape page. The owner wants the business name at the top of every page except the cover, and page numbers that start at 1 on the first chapter.

c3.title: Reminder letters for a Linstead salon
c3.text: A hair salon in Linstead, St Catherine, keeps its clients in a spreadsheet with the columns Title, FirstName, LastName, Address, District, LastVisit and Service. Trainee Shanique is using mail merge to send a reminder letter to every client whose last visit was more than three months ago. The owner, Mrs Pauline Clarke, will review the letter before it goes out.

c4.title: Induction slides at a Runaway Bay hotel
c4.text: Front-office supervisor Mr Jermaine Allen at a hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann, asks trainee Kadian to finish a 15-slide induction presentation for new staff. Every slide must show the hotel's logo in one corner. Several slides have long paragraphs in 14 pt type, and each bullet point flies in with a different animation. Mr Allen wants to see his reminders while he talks, without the audience seeing them.

c5.title: A customer database in Port Antonio
c5.text: An appliance and electrical repair shop in Port Antonio, Portland, keeps a database with a Customers table (CustomerID, Name, Phone, District, Parish) and a Jobs table (JobID, CustomerID, Date, Appliance, Charge in J$). Trainee Garth enters new customers and prepares lists for the owner, Mr Lloyd Bennett.

questions.q: Odette wants E2 to work out the discount on line 2 and then be copied down to E15. Which formula should she type in E2?
questions.why: D2 must change to D3, D4 and so on as the formula is copied, so it stays relative. F2 holds the one discount rate for every line, so it is made absolute with $ signs. =D2*F2 would become =D3*F3 in the next row and point to an empty cell.

questions.q: To add GCT to the subtotal, Odette types =D17+D17*F1. A classmate says it should be =(D17+D17)*F1. Who is right, and why?
o: The classmate, because a formula is worked out from left to right
Both, because brackets make no difference to the answer
Neither, because a formula cannot use the same cell twice
Odette, because multiplication is done before addition
questions.why: Spreadsheets do multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, so Odette's formula adds the GCT amount (D17 × F1) to the subtotal. The classmate's version doubles the subtotal first and then works out only a percentage of that.

questions.q: In a cell meant to show the average cost per outlet, Odette sees #DIV/0!. What is the most likely cause?
o: The column is too narrow to show the whole answer
The cell she divides by is empty or holds zero
The function name has been spelt wrongly in the formula
The formula points to a cell that has been deleted
questions.why: #DIV/0! means the formula is dividing by zero, usually because the cell it divides by, such as the number of outlets, is still empty. A narrow column shows #####, a misspelt function #NAME? and a deleted cell #REF!.

questions.q: Mr Dixon asks how many of the 14 items have a unit price over J$5,000. Which formula gives the answer?
questions.why: COUNTIF counts only the cells in a range that meet a condition, written in quotation marks. SUMIF would add up those prices instead of counting them, COUNT takes no condition, and IF tests a value and gives Yes or No, not a count.

questions.q: Staff keep typing the unit in column G as 'm', 'mtr', 'metre' or 'metres'. How can Odette make everyone choose from the same short list?
o: Freeze the panes, so that the heading of column G is always on view
Use data validation to give column G a drop-down list of units
Use conditional formatting to colour any unit that is spelt wrongly
Sort the sheet by column G, so that the same units are together
questions.why: Data validation limits what can be typed in a cell, for example to a drop-down list such as 'each', 'm' and 'box'. Entries stay the same, so sorting, filtering and counting work properly.

questions.q: Damion made each chapter title bold and 16 pt by hand. When he inserts an automatic table of contents, it is empty. Why?
o: The titles are not in a heading style, so it finds none
The contents page must be typed in by hand in a booklet
Bold text cannot appear in an automatic table of contents
The table of contents works only in documents over 20 pages
questions.why: An automatic table of contents is built from text in heading styles. Hand formatting looks like a heading but the program does not know it is one. Apply Heading 1 to the chapter titles, then update the table.

questions.q: Only page 9, with the wide price table, should be landscape. What must Damion do?
o: Turn the whole booklet to landscape, then shrink the other pages
Make the table's text very small so that it fits on a portrait page
Put the table in its own section and make that section landscape
Insert ordinary page breaks around the table and rotate that page
questions.why: Orientation belongs to a section. Section breaks before and after the table make it a section of its own, which can be landscape while the rest stays portrait. An ordinary page break does not start a new section.

questions.q: How can Damion leave the cover without a header and number, and start the page numbers at 1 on the first chapter?
o: Type the page numbers by hand, starting from the first chapter
Delete the header from the cover, and the numbers will shift themselves
Put the cover, contents and chapters in three separate files
Add a section break after the contents, unlink it and restart at 1
questions.why: A section break after the contents lets the chapters have their own header and footer. Turning off 'Link to Previous' stops changes copying back to the cover, and the page number format can restart at 1. Use Different First Page for the cover.

questions.q: Damion must change every 'tank' to 'cylinder', but the booklet also mentions 'tankless' heaters. What is the safest way?
o: Use Replace All without options; it skips the longer words
Use the spelling checker and change each word as it is found
Use Find and Replace with 'Find whole words only' turned on
Read every page and retype each 'tank' that he can see
questions.why: 'Find whole words only' changes 'tank' but leaves 'tankless' alone. Without it, Replace All would turn 'tankless' into 'cylinderless'. Read the result afterwards; Ctrl+Z undoes a Replace All.

questions.q: In the preview, one letter begins 'Dear Miss ,'. What is the most likely cause?
o: That client's FirstName cell is empty in the data source
The merge field was typed in by hand, not inserted
The letter has too many merge fields for one page
The preview always leaves out the last name of each client
questions.why: A blank in a merged letter almost always comes from a blank in the data source. Fill in the missing detail in the spreadsheet, or correct the column it was typed in, then preview again. Fix the list, not each letter.

questions.q: Only clients whose last visit was more than three months ago should get the letter. How should Shanique do this?
o: Merge all the letters, then pick out the right ones by hand
Sort the list by LastName so the oldest visits come first
Delete the recent clients from the salon's master spreadsheet
Filter the recipients on the LastVisit field before merging
questions.why: Mail merge can filter recipients on any field, so only the rows that meet the condition are merged. The master list stays complete; deleting clients from it would lose their details.

questions.q: Mrs Clarke edits the letter with Track Changes on, and adds a comment: 'Is this price still right?'. What should Shanique do to get a clean final copy?
o: Accept or reject each change, deal with the comment, then turn tracking off
Turn off the markup display so that the changes no longer show, then save
Copy all the text into a new document, which removes every change and comment
Print the letter, since tracked changes and comments never appear on paper
questions.why: Hiding the markup leaves the changes and comment in the file, where a client could still see them. Each change must be accepted or rejected and each comment answered and deleted; then tracking is turned off and the final version saved.

questions.q: How can Kadian put the logo on all 15 slides, and on any slides added later, in one step?
o: Paste the logo onto each slide in turn and line them up
Use the logo as a transition between the slides
Put the logo in the speaker notes of the first slide
Put the logo on the slide master
questions.why: Anything placed on the slide master appears on every slide that uses it, including new slides, and stays in exactly the same position. Pasting it slide by slide is slow and easy to get wrong.

questions.q: What should Kadian do with the slides that have long paragraphs in 14 pt type?
o: Make the text 10 pt, so that more of the paragraph fits on each slide
Keep them as they are, because new staff need every word on the screen
Cut them to a few short points in larger type, with detail in the notes
Add a bright picture behind the text to make the slides more interesting
questions.why: An audience cannot read long, small text and listen at the same time. A few short points in large type, with strong contrast, keep attention on the speaker, and the detail goes in the speaker notes or a handout.

questions.q: How can Mr Allen see his reminders while the audience sees only the slides?
o: Use presenter view, with his notes on the laptop screen
Type the reminders in small print at the foot of each slide
Print the slides as handouts and give them to the audience
Put the reminders in the slide footer in a light colour
questions.why: Presenter view shows the speaker notes, the next slide and a timer on the laptop, while the projector shows only the current slide. Anything typed on a slide itself, however small or pale, is seen by the audience.

questions.q: What should Kadian do about the animations?
o: Give every point a different effect to keep the audience awake
Use one simple effect, only where showing points in turn helps
Remove all of them, since animation is never allowed at work
Change them into transitions, which work the same way
questions.why: Animations should help the message, for example by showing points one at a time as they are discussed. Many different effects distract people. Transitions are different: they work between slides, not on items.

questions.q: Which data type should Garth use for the Phone field in the Customers table?
o: Number, because phone numbers are made up of digits
Currency, so that the digits are grouped neatly
Text, as phone numbers are not used in any sums
Date/Time, so that numbers can be sorted by age
questions.why: A phone number is a label, not an amount. As text it keeps brackets, dashes, a leading plus or zero, and the (876) area code, exactly as typed. Number fields are for values used in calculations.

questions.q: Mr Bennett wants a list of every refrigerator job since 1 June. What should Garth make?
o: A form showing one job record at a time on the screen
A report built straight on the Customers table alone
A new table, with the fridge jobs typed in again by hand
A query with criteria on the Appliance and Date fields
questions.why: A query picks out the records that meet conditions on one or more fields, here Appliance = Refrigerator and Date on or after 1 June. It can be saved and run again, and a report can be built on it for printing.

questions.q: A welding shop's monthly report has a chart pasted from its sales workbook as an embedded object. The figures in the workbook change, but the chart in the report does not. Why?
o: The workbook was saved, which always breaks the chart's link
An embedded chart keeps the data it had when it was pasted
Charts can only be updated when they are pasted as a picture
The report needs printing before the chart can update itself
questions.why: An embedded object is a copy stored inside the report; it does not follow the source file. To make the chart follow the workbook, paste it as a linked object (Paste Special, Paste link) and keep both files in place.

questions.q: A small fabrication shop keeps all its quotes and invoices on one office computer. Which backup plan is best?
o: A copy in another folder on the same computer's hard drive
A copy on a flash drive kept in the drawer next to the computer
Copies on an external drive kept off site and in cloud storage
Printing everything once a year and filing the paper copies
questions.why: A backup must survive whatever destroys the original: a hard-drive failure, theft, a virus, a surge or a flood. Copies on different kinds of storage, one away from the office, follow the 3-2-1 idea. Check now and then that a file can be restored.
